```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(width = 90, digits = 3)
```

```{r setup}
library(bmassa)
```

bmassa estimates the biomass of the taxa of a survey (phytoplankton,
zooplankton, macroinvertebrates, fish and amphibians) from their
abundances, with prediction intervals. For each taxon it predicts the mean
individual mass of a population, from its mean length when there is one and
from typical masses otherwise, with hierarchical models fitted to published
compilations and data sets. A taxon without reference data of its own is
predicted from its closest relatives, and its interval widens accordingly.

Masses are in the native currency of each group: biovolume (µm³) for
phytoplankton, dry mass (mg; molluscs without shell) for invertebrates and
wet mass (g) for fish and amphibians. `convert_currency()` expresses them in
another currency, such as carbon or energy, with the uncertainty of the
conversion.

The workflow:

1. `standardize_taxa()`: the classification of the taxa in the Catalogue of
   Life (needs internet).
2. `check_coverage()`: from which taxonomic level each taxon will be
   estimated, and how wide its interval will be.
3. `estimate_biomass()`: mean individual mass and biomass of each row.
4. `convert_currency()`: another currency, if needed.
5. `summarize_biomass()`: totals by site or any grouping.
6. `cite_sources()`: what to cite.

The example data (`example_survey`) are constructed for two sites of a lake;
they are not field data.

## Input tables

**Taxa**: one row per taxon unit, that is, a taxon or a taxon in one life
stage and sex (the larvae and the adults of a frog are two units), with its
broad group and its classification by main ranks (`NA` below the rank
identified; `species` is the full binomial). Optional columns:

- `col_id`, the identifier of the taxon in the Catalogue of Life (COL XR):
  when present, the taxon is looked up by it first;
- `life_stage` and `sex`;
- `count_unit`, required in phytoplankton: `"cell"` or `"natural_unit"`
  (colony or filament as counted);
- the mean length of the unit in all the samples (`length_mean`,
  `length_unit`, `length_type`), where it was measured, with its spread
  (`length_sd` or `length_cv`), which corrects the mass of the mean length,
  smaller than the mean mass.

```{r taxa}
tx <- example_survey$taxa
tx[, c("taxon_id", "broad_group", "genus", "species", "life_stage", "count_unit",
       "length_mean", "length_unit", "length_type")]
```

**Abundances**: one row per sample and unit: `site` (and `date`, for sites
sampled on several dates), `taxon_id`, `abundance` and `per`, the unit of
area or volume of the abundance. A zero is a unit looked for and not seen;
`NA`, one not counted. Other columns, such as the treatment or the habitat,
are kept.

```{r abundance}
ab <- example_survey$abundance
head(ab)
ab[ab$site == "L2" & ab$taxon_id %in% c("t05", "t08"), ]
```

**Lengths of particular samples** (optional): mean lengths measured in a
site (and date), which take precedence over the length of the unit there.
Here the chub, measured in each site:

```{r lengths}
ln <- example_survey$lengths
ln
```

## Names and classification

`standardize_taxa()` sends each name to the name-matching service of GBIF
and returns the classification of the Catalogue of Life eXtended Release,
the accepted name and its identifier. It replaces synonyms, accepts an
epithet with another ending (*Chironomus plumosa* for *plumosus*), places
"Genus sp." and "Genus cf. species" in the genus, and does not correct
misspelt names: a species it cannot accept is placed in its genus, with the
closest name in `note`. It needs internet, so it is not run here:

```{r standardize, eval = FALSE}
my_taxa <- data.frame(taxon_id = c("a", "b", "c", "d"),
                      broad_group = c("macroinvertebrate", "macroinvertebrate", "zooplankton",
                                      "macroinvertebrate"),
                      scientific_name = c("Baetis rhodani", "Ephemerella ignita", "Daphnia magnaa",
                                          "Chironomus sp."))
s <- standardize_taxa(my_taxa)
#> Querying the Catalogue of Life (COL XR) through the GBIF API for 4 names...
s[, c("scientific_name", "col_name", "genus", "match_type")]
#>      scientific_name          col_name      genus  match_type
#> 1     Baetis rhodani    Baetis rhodani     Baetis       exact
#> 2 Ephemerella ignita Serratella ignita Serratella       exact
#> 3     Daphnia magnaa           Daphnia    Daphnia higher_rank
#> 4     Chironomus sp.        Chironomus Chironomus       exact
s$note[2:3]
#> [1] "Ephemerella ignita is a synonym of Serratella ignita"
#> [2] "species not found in the COL XR: placed in its genus; closest name: Daphnia magna (species, not used)"
```

(Output of a run on 2026-11-02 with the COL26.6 XR.) Check the rows with a
`note` before going on, and keep the result with your data: a new release of
the COL XR may change names. Its result is the classification of the taxa
table; add the counting unit of the phytoplankton and, where they apply, the
stage, sex and mean length of each unit.

## Before estimating: coverage

`check_coverage()` says, for each taxon and way of estimating it, which node
of the reference the estimate will come from and the factor by which the
median is divided and multiplied to get the 95 % interval of a new
population.

```{r coverage}
cov <- check_coverage(tx, ln)
cov
cv <- as.data.frame(cov)
cv[cv$taxon_id %in% c("t01", "t03", "t08", "t13", "t16", "t17"),
   c("taxon_id", "method", "count_unit", "site", "match_level", "match_name", "factor")]
```

Masses without lengths are much more uncertain than masses at a given
length: a typical mass says little about a population whose sizes are not
known. Where lengths can be measured, they narrow the intervals more than a
finer identification does.

## Mean individual mass and biomass

With lengths, the back-transformation of the length-mass relations has to
be chosen: `"none"` gives the median mass of the individuals of a given
length, `"lognormal"` their mean (Sprugel 1983), which is what biomass needs.
There is no default.

```{r estimate}
est <- estimate_biomass(ab, tx, ln, bias_correction = "lognormal")
est
e <- as.data.frame(est)
e[e$site == "L1", c("taxon_id", "method", "match_level", "ind_median", "ind_lower",
                    "ind_upper", "unit")]
```

The interval is a prediction interval for the mean individual mass of a
new population of the taxon. It includes the uncertainty of the model
estimates, of the taxonomic substitution (the levels missing below the node
used), and the variation between populations and between sources; it does
not include the error of the abundances. The rows that could not be
estimated keep `NA`, with the reason:

```{r not-estimated}
ne <- e[e$status != "estimated", ]
ne[, c("site", "taxon_id", "life_stage")]
unique(ne$reason)
```

Some decisions behind those rows, which you can change through the data:

- Fish without lengths are estimated as whole populations: the model is
  fitted to the mean mass of the populations of an electrofishing survey of
  Iberian streams (Arranz et al. 2022) and of the catch of a river fishery
  (Koning et al. 2024), all sizes together, so its intervals are wide; a mean
  length gives a much closer estimate. A fish of an order absent from those
  data takes the mean of all of them, and a fish given a life stage or a sex
  is not estimated without a length.
- Phytoplankton counted in natural units (colonies, filaments) takes the
  natural units of the reference, which in colonial genera are often single
  cells or small groups of their sources, not whole colonies (a note says
  so); give `cells_per_unit` in `taxa` when the cells of a unit were
  counted, and the unit is estimated as that many cells.
- Rotifers are predicted as from volumes, the usual method of field studies;
  direct weighings of their dry mass, about four times as heavy, enter the
  model as a fixed contrast.
- Benthic invertebrates are predicted as means of field populations (Hrycik
  et al. 2024); the masses of individual prey compiled by Moreau et al.
  (2021), about six times as heavy for the same taxa, enter the model as a
  fixed contrast.
- Insects without a stage are taken as larvae (`stage_used = "larva
  (assumed)"`); give `life_stage = "adult"` (or `"pupa"`) in `taxa` otherwise.
- Copepods without a stage are taken as adults (`stage_used =
  "copepod_adult (assumed)"`); copepodites and nauplii (`life_stage =
  "copepodite"` or `"nauplius"`) are about 2.7 and 33 times lighter, with
  fixed contrasts estimated from few records of nauplii, hence their wide
  intervals. A copepod given as `"juvenile"` is not estimated.
- Amphibians without lengths are estimated only when declared adults.
- A length outside the range of the reference relations of the taxon and
  its relatives is not estimated unless `extrapolate = TRUE`.

The intervals of the animals of site L1, in mg (the masses of fish and
amphibians, in g, multiplied by 1000):

```{r plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, fig.alt = "Median and 95 % prediction interval of the mean individual mass of each animal taxon at site L1, in mg on a log scale: narrow for the taxa with lengths, wide for those without"}
l1 <- e[e$site == "L1" & !is.na(e$ind_median) & e$unit != "um3", ]
to_mg <- ifelse(l1$unit == "g", 1000, 1)
l1[c("ind_median", "ind_lower", "ind_upper")] <- l1[c("ind_median", "ind_lower", "ind_upper")] * to_mg
l1 <- l1[order(l1$ind_median), ]
y <- seq_len(nrow(l1))
col <- ifelse(l1$method == "length", "black", "grey55")
op <- par(mar = c(4, 11, 1, 1))
plot(l1$ind_median, y, log = "x", xlim = range(l1$ind_lower, l1$ind_upper), pch = 19, col = col,
     yaxt = "n", ylab = "", xlab = "Mean individual mass (mg)")
segments(l1$ind_lower, y, l1$ind_upper, y, col = col)
axis(2, at = y, labels = l1$scientific_name, las = 1, cex.axis = 0.75, font = 3)
legend("topleft", c("from its length", "without length"), col = c("black", "grey55"), pch = 19,
       lty = 1, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
par(op)
```

## Other currencies

`convert_currency()` converts with hierarchical models of the conversion
factors (ratios of dry to wet mass, ash-free dry mass to dry mass, carbon to
dry mass...) fitted to the data of Brey et al. (2010), Hrycik et al.
(2024), Coughlan et al. (2021), Evans-White et al. (2005) and the CADSES
data sets. A taxon gets the factor of its closest relatives, and the
uncertainty of the factor adds to that of the mass. Factors measured on
animals kept in ethanol or formalin were left out where the source says so:
preservation changes their wet and dry mass by amounts that depend on the
preservative, the time and the species (Dermott and Paterson 1974).
Phytoplankton biovolumes go to wet mass with the density of
water, 1 g/cm3 (1 mm3/L = 1 mg/L), the convention of EN 16695 and of most
monitoring programmes; measured densities of algal cells are up to 10 %
higher (Oliver et al. 1981), an uncertainty not included. Rotifers, which have
no wet to dry mass factors in the reference data, go to wet mass with the
convention of US EPA (2016): dry mass 10 % of the wet mass (3.9 % in
*Asplanchna*, after Dumont et al. 1975). Amphibians, which have too few
factors in the reference data for a model, go between wet and dry mass with
the water content of frogs and toads compiled by US EPA (1993; mean of three
studies): 85 % (SD 4.7), so a dry mass of 15 % of the wet mass on average,
with that spread among populations and the uncertainty of the mean added to
the interval (salamanders and newts get it as an extrapolation).
Phytoplankton cells (and natural units with `cells_per_unit`) are converted
to carbon with the equations of Menden-Deuer and Lessard (2000), whose own
uncertainty is not known (only that of the biovolume is carried). A common
unit is needed to compare groups:

```{r carbon}
est_c <- convert_currency(est, to = "carbon", unit = "ug")
ec <- as.data.frame(est_c)
ec[ec$site == "L1", c("taxon_id", "converted_from", "ind_median", "ind_lower", "ind_upper",
                      "unit", "status")]
unique(ec$conversion[!is.na(ec$conversion)])[1:4]
```

Amphibians are not converted to ash-free dry mass or carbon: the reference
data have too few conversion factors for them. Phytoplankton counted in
natural units is not converted to carbon unless `taxa` gives its
`cells_per_unit`: the equation is for single cells, and applied to a colony
it would underestimate its carbon. Natural units do go to wet mass, which is
proportional to the biovolume. The habitat of the organisms (`habitat`) is
unknown by default; its variance is then added.

Energy (J, or `"mJ"`, `"kJ"`, `"MJ"`) comes from models of energy per dry
mass (invertebrates) and per wet mass (fish) fitted to the energy densities of
Brey et al. (2010), Cummins and Wuycheck (1971) and other articles, screened
first: values per ash-free dry mass outside 15-45 J/mg (the combustion energy
of carbohydrate, protein and lipid sets 17.5-39.5 J/mg; Gnaiger and
Bitterlich 1984), values inconsistent with another value of the same
material and values far from those of their class were left out. These are
gross energies of whole animals, not the energy a consumer assimilates.
Amphibians take the energy per dry mass of frogs and toads compiled by US
EPA (1993), 4.6 kcal/g (19.2 J/mg; SD 0.45, three studies). Phytoplankton
goes to energy from its carbon with the general factor of Platt and Irwin
(1973), 11.40 cal (47.7 J) per mg of carbon (SD 1.1 among their 10 samples),
measured on marine net phytoplankton of a spring bloom: for freshwater
phytoplankton it is an extrapolation, which the rows note.

```{r energy}
est_e <- convert_currency(est, to = "energy", unit = "J")
ee <- as.data.frame(est_e)
ee[ee$site == "L1" & ee$status == "estimated",
   c("taxon_id", "converted_from", "ind_median", "ind_lower", "ind_upper", "biomass_unit")]
```

## Totals

`summarize_biomass()` adds up the biomass by site, broad group or any other
grouping, never across currencies or units. The interval of a total comes
from simulations in which the rows that share a node of the reference (two
species estimated from the same family), a missing taxon, a population or a
conversion factor share the same draws: their errors are correlated, and the
totals reflect it.

```{r totals}
tot <- summarize_biomass(est_c, by = c("site", "broad_group"), na_rm = TRUE, seed = 1)
tot[, c("site", "broad_group", "biomass_unit", "biomass_mean", "biomass_lower",
        "biomass_upper", "n_missing")]
```

- `na_rm = FALSE` (default) leaves a total `NA` when any of its rows has no
  biomass; with `TRUE` the total is that of the rows estimated (a lower
  bound), and `n_missing` says how many were left out.
- `biomass_mean` is exact (the sum of the means of the rows); the median and
  the limits come from the draws and change slightly with the seed. With the
  default 1000 draws, the limits of these totals vary by up to about 13 %
  between seeds; use `n_draws = 10000` for final results.
- `population_effect = "shared"` (default) takes the variation between
  populations as common to all the sites (the sites of a study usually share
  populations and season); `"independent"` draws it per row. It does not
  change the total of one site, but it does change sums over sites and
  differences between them. With `population_by`, the populations are shared
  only within the groups of some columns of the abundance table: habitats
  stocked from different water bodies, or regions, have their own.
- `seed` makes the draws reproducible and restores the random state of the
  session afterwards.

## A common basis

Biomasses per litre and per square metre cannot be added up. To add the
groups of a site, as the nodes of a food web, `convert_abundance()` puts
all the abundances on one basis before estimating: per a volume, per an
area or per whole site. `per` gives the size of each sample (`"L"`,
`"5 L"`, `"0.25 m2"`...), and a table of sites gives what the conversion
needs: the depth (or the volume and the area) to go between volumes and
areas, and the volume or the area to go to the total of a site, as in
mesocosms. Here everything per square metre, with the mean depth of each
site:

```{r basis}
sites <- data.frame(site = c("L1", "L2"), depth = c(1.5, 0.8), depth_unit = "m")
ab_m2 <- convert_abundance(ab, to = "m2", sites = sites)
unique(ab_m2[, c("per_original", "per", "per_factor", "per_assumption")])
```

Going from volume to area takes the density of the sample as that of the
whole water column; `per_assumption` says so in every row. Counts of
semi-quantitative samples (sweep nets, artificial substrates) have no area of
their own: the one given in `per` is an assumption.

## Draws for other models

Models that use the biomass of every taxon, such as the energy fluxes of a
food web, need the draws themselves: `simulate()` gives, for every row and
draw, the mean individual mass and the biomass, with the same shared errors
as the totals (with the same seed, they are the draws behind
`summarize_biomass()`). Compute the quantity of interest in each draw and
summarise it over the draws: the correlations between rows are kept, so a
difference between two sites where a taxon has the same population reflects
its abundances, not the uncertainty of its mass. Here each habitat has its
own populations, and all groups are in wet mass in mg per square metre:

```{r simulate, warning = FALSE}
ab_m2$habitat <- ifelse(ab_m2$site == "L1", "lake", "spring")
est_w <- convert_currency(estimate_biomass(ab_m2, tx, ln, bias_correction = "lognormal"),
                          to = "wet_mass", unit = "mg")
sim <- simulate(est_w, nsim = 1000, seed = 1, population_by = "habitat")
sim
d <- as.data.frame(sim, draws = 1:2)
head(d[, c("draw", "site", "taxon_id", "habitat", "ind_mass", "biomass", "biomass_unit")])
```

- The long table has one row per row and draw; `draws` takes a subset, and
  `sim$ind_mass` is the matrix of masses (rows by draws).
- The abundances are taken as known, and each row has the mean mass of its
  population: a taxon without lengths has the same distribution of mass in
  every site and date.

## What to cite

```{r sources}
knitr::kable(cite_sources(est_c)[, c("source_id", "licence", "n_rows")])
```

`get_reference()` returns the reference tables themselves: the models, their
nodes and variance components, the conversion models and the sources.

## How the models were fitted and checked

The models were fitted outside the package with lme4 (REML), one per domain
and kind of data: masses without lengths with nested random intercepts by
taxonomic level, crossed with the source (except in invertebrates, whose
sources measure different groups of taxa by different methods, so that each
taxon keeps the level of the sources that measured it); length-mass
relations with random
intercepts and slopes by taxonomic level within each type of length, from
three points of each equation inside its range of lengths, with effects of
equation and study; conversion factors with nested random intercepts and
crossed effects of habitat and source. The package keeps, for each node of
each model, the estimate of its path from the root and its conditional
variance (and its covariance with the path of its parent, which the
simulation of totals needs), and predicts with base R.

In cross-validation (scripts in `dev/validacion/` of the source repository),
the 95 % intervals covered 93-97 % of new populations of species in the
reference and 91-97 % of species left out, in the eight models. The median
width of the interval for a new population of a species of the reference
was:

| Model | Median 95 % factor (×/÷) |
|---|---|
| Fish, length-mass | 1.2 |
| Amphibians, length-mass | 1.8 |
| Invertebrates, length-mass | 3.7 |
| Amphibians, adult masses | 6.4 |
| Fish, mean mass of populations without lengths | 8.9 |
| Invertebrates, dry mass without lengths | 14 |
| Phytoplankton, cell biovolume | 20 |
| Phytoplankton, natural-unit biovolume | 38 |

## From version 0.1.0

The functions and data sets of 0.1.0 (`typical_mass`, `length_mass`,
`carbon_volume`, `taxonomy`, `example_counts` and `example_lengths`) were
removed in 0.2.0. What replaces each function:

| 0.1.0 | 0.2.0 |
|---|---|
| `match_taxa()` | `check_coverage()` |
| `estimate_mass_typical()`, `estimate_mass_length()`, `calc_biomass()` | `estimate_biomass()` |
| `calc_phyto_carbon()`, `convert_currency()` with factors | `convert_currency()` on an estimate |
| `read_brey_databank()` | not needed: the factors of Brey et al. (2010) are in the conversion models |
| `summarize_biomass()` of `calc_biomass()` | `summarize_biomass()` of an estimate |

Masses are now in mg (invertebrates) and g (vertebrates), not µg, and come
from the hierarchical models rather than from the reference values of the
taxon or its relatives.
